title: Lister's antiseptic surgery

confidence.note: Lister's own 1867 papers fix the dates, from the first carbolic dressing in August 1865 to publication in 1867. That antisepsis cut wound infection is accepted; how quickly and why it spread is debated, and historians now stress that his critics had serious reasons for doubt.

people: Joseph Lister (1827–1912), professor of surgery at Glasgow
James Greenlees, boy whose compound fracture was the first case in Lister's 1867 series
Thomas Anderson (1819–1874), Glasgow chemist who pointed Lister to Pasteur's work
summary: A Glasgow surgeon read Pasteur, reasoned that germs rot wounds, and dressed a boy's open fracture in carbolic acid. Making the idea stick took decades.
body: On 12 August 1865 an eleven-year-old boy, James Greenlees, was admitted to the Glasgow Royal Infirmary with a compound fracture: the broken bone had pierced the skin, so that infection was likely and healing imperfect. Such wounds often ended in amputation. Joseph Lister dressed the wound with a pad soaked in carbolic acid. It did not suppurate.

Lister was acting on a borrowed idea. The Glasgow chemist Thomas Anderson had introduced him to Louis Pasteur's work showing that fermentation and putrefaction were caused by living organisms carried in the air, not by oxygen itself. If so, Lister reasoned, wounds need not be sealed from the air; it was enough to kill the "floating particles" with a chemical dressing.

He published in *The Lancet* in the spring of 1867, in four weekly articles describing eleven compound fractures, failures included, followed by a fifth on abscesses. Later that year he told the British Medical Association in Dublin that his two wards, once among the unhealthiest in the infirmary, had gone nine months without a single case of pyemia, hospital gangrene or erysipelas.

Acceptance was slow. A leading Leeds surgeon, Thomas Nunneley, reported that his colleagues had tried the method and given it up. Lister kept changing his materials, carbolic acid itself irritated tissue, and the germ theory behind it was not yet proven. Historians now argue that every part of the system was contested for good reasons, not out of ignorance.

The next step came from Germany. Robert Koch's laboratory found carbolic acid a weak germicide and Lister's spray useless, and surgeons turned to steam sterilization and keeping germs out of the wound altogether. In 1890 Ernst von Bergmann announced that his clinic had replaced antisepsis with asepsis, the principle of the modern operating room.

myth.tradition: Lister's critics were hidebound reactionaries who refused to believe in germs, and his method was obviously right from the start.
myth.record: His contemporaries had real grounds for doubt: results varied, the technique kept changing and the bacteriology was unsettled. Much of his system, including the carbolic spray, was later dropped in favor of asepsis.

links.note: Lister applied Pasteur's account of putrefaction to wounds.

title: The thermometer and the fever chart

confidence.note: Wunderlich's treatise appeared in Leipzig in 1868 and in English in 1871. The figure of about 25,000 cases comes from later summaries of his work, and whether his 37 °C was too high, or body temperature has since fallen, is still argued.

people: Carl Reinhold August Wunderlich (1815–1877), Leipzig physician
Thomas Clifford Allbutt (1836–1925), Leeds physician who devised a short clinical thermometer
summary: A Leipzig doctor charted the temperatures of some 25,000 patients and turned fever from a feeling into a number, with 37 °C as the healthy norm.
body: In 1868 Carl Wunderlich of Leipzig published a treatise on temperature in disease, drawn from about 15 years of readings, some patients measured four to six times a day. Plotted on charts, he argued, fevers followed characteristic courses, while healthy temperature held steady near 37 °C. His thermometers were large and slow, sometimes needing 20 minutes; in Leeds, Clifford Allbutt's 15-centimeter clinical thermometer, made from 1867, gave a reading in about five. Modern studies put average healthy temperature somewhat lower.

myth.tradition: Normal body temperature is exactly 37 °C, or 98.6 °F.
myth.record: Wunderlich gave a normal range of about 36.2–37.5 °C, and a recent British study of more than 35,000 patients found a mean oral temperature of 36.6 °C.

title: Robert Koch hunts the microbes

confidence.note: Koch's papers and the record of his 1882 lecture fix the key dates, and his identification of the anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera bacteria is not in doubt. What is often blurred is how much was his alone: earlier observers had seen the anthrax and cholera organisms, and the postulates were codified by his assistant.

place: Wollstein (now Wolsztyn, Poland) and Berlin, Germany
people: Robert Koch (1843–1910), German physician and bacteriologist
Friedrich Loeffler, Koch's assistant, who set out the postulates in 1883
Walther and Fanny Hesse, assistants who suggested agar as a culture medium
Rudolf Virchow, pathologist, early skeptic and critic of tuberculin
summary: A country doctor with a microscope from his wife proved that particular bacteria cause particular diseases, found the killer behind tuberculosis, then overreached with a cure.
body: On 24 March 1882 Robert Koch told the Physiological Society in Berlin that he had found the cause of tuberculosis, a disease many then believed to be hereditary. Using new staining methods he had shown rod-shaped bacteria in tubercular tissue and grown them in pure culture. Some listeners, Rudolf Virchow among them, were at first unconvinced.

Koch had begun as a district medical officer in the small town of Wollstein, working in his four-room flat with a microscope his wife had given him. Others had already seen the anthrax bacillus; Koch grew it in pure culture for generation after generation, away from any animal, and showed it still caused anthrax. Published in 1876, the work made him famous and took him to Berlin.

There his group made bacteriology a routine technique. Assistants Walther and Fanny Hesse suggested agar as a solid medium in 1881, and the flat dish of his colleague Petri followed. The test now called Koch's postulates, set out in classic form by his assistant Friedrich Loeffler in 1883, asked that a microbe be found in every case, grown in pure culture, and reproduce the disease when inoculated. In 1883–84 Koch led a cholera commission to Egypt and India, growing the comma-shaped vibrio in pure culture in Calcutta on 7 January 1884. The Italian Filippo Pacini had described it in 1854, and because healthy people can carry it, cholera never fitted the postulates neatly.

Then came overreach. In 1890 Koch announced that tuberculin, an extract of tubercle bacilli, could arrest tuberculosis. Excitement ran ahead of the evidence: the cure was greatly exaggerated, and in January 1891 Virchow reported autopsies of 21 patients who had died soon after treatment. Koch's reputation suffered, though tuberculin survived as a diagnostic skin test. He received the Nobel Prize in 1905.

myth.tradition: Koch discovered the bacteria of anthrax and cholera and laid down his famous postulates, which his work perfectly satisfied.
myth.record: Both organisms had been seen before him; his achievement was proving cause through pure culture and inoculation. The postulates were formalized by Loeffler, and cholera, carried by healthy people, broke the rule that the microbe must be absent from the well.

links.note: Pasteur's rival program made germs a cause of disease.
Behring and Kitasato worked in Koch's institute.
A later, more durable weapon against tuberculosis.

title: Pasteur's laboratory vaccines

confidence.note: The dates of Pouilly-le-Fort and of Joseph Meister's treatment are well documented. Pasteur's 152 laboratory notebooks, studied by Gerald Geison and others, show that his public accounts concealed how the anthrax vaccine was made and how little testing preceded the rabies treatment; how harshly to judge this is still debated.

people: Louis Pasteur (1822–1895), chemist and microbiologist
Henri Toussaint (1847–1890), veterinarian who made an earlier anthrax vaccine
Joseph Meister (1876–1940), nine-year-old bitten by a rabid dog
Joseph Grancher, physician who gave the rabies injections
summary: Pasteur turned germs into vaccines against chicken cholera, anthrax and rabies. His private notebooks tell a messier story than his public triumphs.
body: In 1880 Louis Pasteur reported a vaccine against chicken cholera, made from a germ the veterinarian Henri Toussaint had sent him. A year later he staked his reputation on a public trial at Pouilly-le-Fort: sheep were vaccinated against anthrax on 5 May 1881, all the animals were injected with virulent anthrax on 31 May, and on 2 June the vaccinated sheep were thriving while the unvaccinated were dead or dying. Pasteur implied the germs had been weakened by exposure to air; in fact his team had used potassium dichromate, a chemical method close to Toussaint's.

On 6 July 1885 nine-year-old Joseph Meister, badly bitten by a rabid dog, was brought from Alsace. He received a course of injections of dried spinal cord from rabid rabbits, each more virulent than the last, and survived. He was not the first person treated: a man in May and a girl, who died, in June preceded him, and the dried-cord method had been tried on only some 40 dogs in the weeks before.

myth.tradition: Pasteur discovered attenuation by chance when an old chicken-cholera culture, forgotten over a summer holiday, failed to kill hens.
myth.record: His notebooks have no entries for the supposed months and show him still asking in January 1880 when to take the microbe so it could vaccinate.

links.note: Pasteur generalized Jenner's word 'vaccination' to every such preventive.

title: Bismarck's health insurance

confidence.note: The 1881 imperial message and the 1883 Sickness Insurance Act are matters of public record, as are the membership figures. Calling it the first national social insurance scheme is standard; it built on sickness funds that already existed.

people: Otto von Bismarck, German chancellor from 1871
Wilhelm I, German emperor in whose name the program was announced
summary: To draw workers away from socialism, Germany required them to join sickness funds in 1883, creating the employment-based model of health insurance that Germany and other countries still use.
body: When Otto von Bismarck became Germany's chancellor in 1871, hundreds of sickness insurance funds already existed. Alarmed by the workers' movement, he pushed to extend them to workers in low-wage occupations, and in 1883 the Sickness Insurance Act obliged covered workers to join, the first social insurance program organized on a national level. The motive was openly political. An imperial message read by Bismarck to the Reichstag on 17 November 1881 said social ills must be cured not only by repressing the Social Democrats, already banned under the Anti-Socialist Law of 1878, but by promoting workers' welfare.

The funds grew fast: about 4.3 million members at the end of 1885, more than 9 million by 1900. Financed by contributions and run without profit, the scheme became the template for the "Bismarck model" of health care. Because cover came through work, it did not reach everyone.

myth.record: Mutual sickness funds were already common; his law made membership compulsory for many workers and organized the system nationally.

links.note: Britain later chose the other model: tax-funded care for all.
An earlier, sanitary approach to the health of the poor.

title: Halsted: gloves, residency and radical surgery

confidence.note: The glove story rests on later accounts and is usually dated to 1890; the residency system took shape at Johns Hopkins in the 1890s; the mastectomy results were published in 1894.

people: William Stewart Halsted (1852–1922), surgeon
Caroline Hampton, scrub nurse, later his wife
summary: The surgeon behind rubber gloves, the surgical residency and the radical mastectomy did much of it while battling an addiction that began with his cocaine experiments.
body: Around 1890 William Halsted had Goodyear make thin rubber gloves for his scrub nurse, Caroline Hampton, whose hands were inflamed by mercuric chloride; only later did surgeons notice that gloves cut infections. At Johns Hopkins he built a pyramidal residency of graduated responsibility and research, and in 1894 reported his radical mastectomy, long the standard operation. Earlier experiments with cocaine in New York had left him addicted.

title: Diphtheria antitoxin

confidence.note: Behring and Kitasato's 1890 paper, the 1901 Nobel award and the 1902 US law are well documented. The early clinical evidence was not randomized, so the size of the benefit in the 1890s rests on comparisons with earlier years.

people: Emil von Behring (1854–1917), German bacteriologist
Kitasato Shibasaburō (1853–1931), Japanese bacteriologist
Émile Roux, Pasteur Institute scientist who tested serum on children
summary: Blood from immunized horses saved children from diphtheria, won the first Nobel Prize in medicine, and, after a contaminated batch killed 13 children, gave the US its first biologics law.
body: In 1890 Emil Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō, working in Robert Koch's Berlin institute, reported that animals given graduated doses of sterilized diphtheria or tetanus cultures made substances in their blood that neutralized the bacterial poison. These antitoxins could protect a second animal and even cure one already sick. Horses were soon immunized to make serum in bulk. In Paris in 1894 Émile Roux and colleagues gave it to 300 children with diphtheria; 26 percent died, against about 50 percent in earlier years at the same hospital, though without a randomized comparison.

In 1901 Behring alone received the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, though Kitasato's part was widely acknowledged. The same year in St. Louis, serum drawn from a retired milk-wagon horse named Jim, which had tetanus, killed 13 children, by the FDA's count. Congress responded with the Biologics Control Act of 1 July 1902, the first federal control over how such products were made.

links.note: The work came out of Koch's institute.
The 1902 law preceded broader US drug regulation in 1906.
Active immunization, where antitoxin gave borrowed immunity.

title: The age of the asylum

confidence.note: The 1845 Acts and Dix's 1843 report are firmly dated; the 'age of the asylum' is a historians' label for a long process, and its rise and decline varied by country.

people: Dorothea Dix, American reformer who campaigned for state asylums
summary: Reformers built asylums to cure madness with kindness. Within decades they had become crowded warehouses for chronic patients.
body: In 1845 the Lunacy Act and County Asylums Act compelled every county in England and Wales to provide an asylum for pauper lunatics, moved out of workhouses, under a national inspecting commission. In the United States, Dorothea Dix's 1843 report to the Massachusetts legislature, urging enlargement of the Worcester asylum, began a campaign that helped found state hospitals across the country. Built for curative "moral treatment," they filled faster than they emptied: Utica admitted 300–500 people a year from 1846 but discharged about 200 recovered or improved, and overcrowding and restraint followed.

links.note: The humane regime the asylums were meant to deliver.
Asylum case records fed the new classifications.
Drugs and policy later emptied the asylums.
